did_you_know.text: Did you know? Ecclesiastes contrasts human beings with God: God is in heaven, while people are on earth. Therefore, he advises people not to be hasty in speaking, but to limit themselves to a few thoughtful words.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes connects an abundance of dreams and concerns with an abundance of words, portraying the fool’s voice as excessive and unrestrained speech.
Did you know? According to Ecclesiastes, a vow is more than a solemn statement: once it has been made, it should be fulfilled promptly, because a vow has no value if it is not carried out.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes says that it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to fulfill it, emphasizing the practical responsibility of anyone who makes a promise.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes warns against using a mistake as an excuse after saying something improper, because speech can provoke God’s anger and bring harm to a person’s work.
Did you know? After mentioning dreams, vanities, and many words, Ecclesiastes sums up the passage with a brief command: “Fear God.”

Did you know? Ecclesiastes describes a society with levels of authority and oversight, one above another. Therefore, he warns people not to be immediately surprised when they see the oppression of the poor and the violation of justice and righteousness.

Did you know? Alongside his description of governing systems, Ecclesiastes mentions the advantage of the land and the king’s dependence on cultivated fields, presenting the soil as essential even to rulers.

Did you know? Ecclesiastes does not present money as a source of satisfaction: whoever loves money will never have enough, and an increase in wealth also brings an increase in the number of people who consume it.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes compares the laborer’s sleep—which is sweet whether he has eaten little or much—with the rich person’s fullness, which may actually keep him from sleeping.
Did you know? Ecclesiastes describes wealth hoarded by its owner to his own harm and warns that accumulated riches do not guarantee security or benefit.
Did you know? In contrast to the pursuit of wealth and anxiety, Ecclesiastes presents the ability to eat, drink, and find satisfaction in one’s work as a person’s “portion” and as a gift from God.
